documentation.range: Aulostomus maculatus is distributed in the tropical western Atlantic Ocean, from the Bahamas and Bermuda, around south Florida, in the Gulf of Mexico from the Florida Keys, offshore banks and reefs in the northern Gulf and off Mexico from Tuxpan along the Yucatan Peninsula to Cuba, throughout the Caribbean Sea, and along the coast of South America to St. Paul's Rocks off Brazil (Bowen et al. 2001, Fritzsche and Vincent 2002, Kuiter 2009). It occurs between 2-50 m depth (Lieske and Myers 1994, R. Robertson pers. comm. 2014).
documentation.population: This species is common throughout its range (Fritzsche 2002, R. Robertson pers. comm. 2013), however it is thought have lost a substantial portion of its main habitat since the 1970s (Jackson et al. 2014). It is common in the lower Florida Keys, but more frequent in the upper Keys (Schmitt and Sullivan 1996).
documentation.habitats:
Aulostomus maculatus is a shallow-dwelling coral/rocky reef fish that lives in clear water, coral habitats and gorgonian and seagrass beds. It feeds mainly on other small fishes and shrimp and commonly grows to 50 cm in length, with a maximum recorded at 100 cm (Fritzsche and Vincent 2002). Juveniles that were aged between 80-94 days off Caribbean Panama measured 8.9-10.4 cm SL (Bowen et al. 2001).

It tends to reside in the branching growth forms of the reefs they live  on because they use the branches as camouflage with their thin, long bodies and can easily stalk their prey (Gratwicke and Speight 2005). Also, this species uses vertical hovering - aligning their bodies vertically with sponges, gorgonians, and other slim objects of similar colouring - and shadow stalking - aligning itself with the dorsal lines of similar coloured fishes - as techniques to capture prey (Baehr 2007). Aulostomus maculatus preys regularly on fishes and is regularly attacked by Eupomacentrus planifrons, but their feeding activity is not inhibited by these attacks. While members of this species are most commonly seen singly, they sometimes associate with Scarus croicensis schools to avoid being attacked by E. planifrons. When they are acting as associates they have higher feeding rates (Robertson et al. 1976).

Observed widespread loss and degradation of corals and seagrasses in the Caribbean leads to an inferred decline in area of occupancy (AOO) for this species, though it is not thought to have exceeded a 30% reduction in three generations.
documentation.threats:
Habitat loss and degradation are the major threats to A. maculatus. Coral reefs and seagrasses are declining globally (Carpenter et al. 2008, Short et al. 2011), as well as in the Caribbean (Alvarez-Filip et al. 2009, Jackson et al. 2014). Historical coral losses have been substantial, on the order of ~80% since the 1970s (Gardner et al. 2003, Jackson et al. 2014). Increased pressures on corals from rising sea surface temperatures (Carpenter et al. 2008), increased extreme weather events (Gardner et al. 2005), ocean acidification (Edmunds et al. 2013), and indirect ecosystem effects of the Lionfish (Pterois volitans) invasion (Lesser and Slattery 2011) are likely to at least have contributed to a further decline if not an acceleration since these publications. Declines are thought to be similar for seagrasses in the Caribbean (Waycott et al. 2009). However, the species is thought to utilize other habitats such as rocky reefs.

This species is a minor component of the aquarium trade and some small fisheries, and has been identified as a prey item of the invasive Lionfish (Morris and Akins 2009, Green and Cote 2014, Bejarano et al. 2014). These are not considered to be major threats to wild populations, although competition with Lionfish may have a detrimental impact on the species (Green et al. 2012).
documentation.measures:
There are no species-specific conservation measures in place for this fish, but its distribution overlaps many marine protected areas. These include frequent occurrences recorded in seven proposed or established Marine Protected Areas off Belize: Bacalcar Chico Marine Reserve, Turneffe Atoll, South Water Cay Marine Reserve, Sapodilla Cays, Snake Cays, and other unspecified areas (Harborne 2000).

Monitoring is needed to establish population size and trends, and to understand how coral and seagrass loss affect the species. International legislation is required to mitigate against effects of climate change on this species' habitat.
documentation.use_trade: It is likely a minor component of the aquarium trade (R. Robertson pers. comm. 2013). Separate catch statistics are not reported for Aulostomus maculatus, but is sought after by minor commercial fishing industries and is often caught in seines and traps. It is marketed fresh locally. Between 1995-2000, 487 specimens were traded as marine aquarium fish in Fortaleza, Ceara, Brazil which composed 0.24% of all the fishes that were recorded in the trade (Monteiro-Neto et al. 2003).
documentation.rationale: Currently Aulostomus maculatus is assessed as Least Concern. Although severe declines have been observed in the majority of habitat types the species occupies, it is able to utilize other habitat types. Its widespread range makes it resilient to localized declines in habitat quality.
documentation.taxonomic_notes: Many specimens historically identified as A. maculatus that have been found off the coast of Brazil around St. Paul's Rocks may have been misidentifications of A. strigosus, which has been recorded there based on molecular evidence (Bowen et al. 2001).
